title: Quantum Simulator Recreates Matter 'Popping Into Existence'
summary:
Researchers at the Duke Quantum Center have used a quantum simulator to observe a bizarre process called string breaking. The work, published September 23 in Nature Physics, shows how trapped ion quantum computers could become powerful tools for exploring fundamental physics.

Quarks are the smallest known building blocks of matter. They're found inside protons and neutrons and are about a billion times smaller than an atom. But you can't just pull a quark out by itself. Quarks are held together by a tight connection — imagine two charged particles linked by a stretched string. The farther apart you pull them, the more energy builds up. Eventually, enough energy accumulates to create new particle pairs. This happens because mass and energy are related through Einstein's famous equation, E=mc².

This process, called string breaking, normally requires extreme conditions — like those inside the Large Hadron Collider or shortly after the Big Bang. But the Duke-led team recreated it using a chain of 13 trapped ions. They used lasers to control how the ions interacted, then watched the system evolve.

"Quantum computer simulations provide the best platform to investigate complex questions like matter formation, short of having witnessed the Big Bang itself," said Christopher Monroe, a professor at Duke who led the research.

Arinjoy De, the study's first author, added that working at the intersection of quantum simulation and high-energy physics is "incredibly exciting." The international team included researchers from the University of Maryland, Oxford University, Caltech, Cornell University and KU Leuven.

The team also modeled the same process on a classical computer, and the results matched. But as experiments grow larger and more complex, quantum computers will eventually solve problems that classical machines cannot. Other groups, including Google and QuEra Computing, have achieved similar milestones using different hardware — superconducting circuits and neutral atoms.

"These are the three platforms leading the charge in quantum computing," Monroe added. The findings open new pathways for understanding matter at its most fundamental level.
why_it_matters: As quantum simulators grow, they could let scientists study conditions — like the matter formed shortly after the Big Bang — that no ordinary laboratory can recreate. The race between hardware platforms also has long-term stakes: whichever approach proves most reliable could shape computing, chemistry and materials research for decades.

background_read: Quarks are the particles inside protons and neutrons. Physicists proposed them because experiments kept showing that protons were not solid balls but had structure inside; today quarks, and the force that binds them, are described by the Standard Model — physics' best account of fundamental particles.

The Large Hadron Collider (the world's biggest particle accelerator, run by CERN near Geneva, where protons are smashed together at nearly the speed of light) has studied quark behaviour at extreme energies. But such machines are enormous and expensive, which is why simpler, controllable systems are attractive.

Quantum simulators take a different route: instead of colliding particles, researchers build a model system they can fully control and let it imitate nature. The Duke Quantum Center is part of Duke University in North Carolina, and its team used trapped ions — charged atoms held by electric fields and manipulated with lasers — as programmable particles.

Nature Physics (a peer-reviewed journal that publishes physics research only after other scientists check it) carried the study. Meanwhile Google, using superconducting circuits, and QuEra Computing, using neutral atoms, have reported similar milestones, so the field is advancing on several hardware tracks at once.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a new instrument for fundamental physics
perspectives.description: Supporters see this as proof that table-top quantum devices can reproduce phenomena once reachable only in giant colliders. That opens high-energy physics to smaller, cheaper labs and lets researchers dial parameters up and down instead of waiting for rare collisions. The involvement of universities across several countries also shows the field is becoming collaborative rather than concentrated.

A sceptic would note that only 13 ions were used, and the result matched a classical simulation, so no new physics was discovered and no quantum advantage was shown. Trapped-ion systems are also sensitive to noise and errors that grow quickly with size. Until simulations beat classical computers on a genuinely unsolved problem, the practical payoff remains a promise.

Physicists have long used one controllable system to imitate another — cold atoms standing in for electrons in a crystal, for example — because some equations are simply too hard to solve directly. This work fits that tradition, applying it to the strong force that binds quarks. The parallel progress by three different hardware platforms suggests the field is exploring several paths rather than betting on one.

The obvious next questions are how many ions or qubits can be linked before errors dominate, and whether error correction can keep larger simulations trustworthy. If it can, simulations could tackle problems in nuclear physics and materials science that classical machines cannot. Funding and talent may then shift toward whichever platform proves most scalable.
